title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E555 interpolates through infinitely many prescribed points (x_k, y_k) using an 'aequatio finita' of Lagrange type, an infinite product divided by a normalising integral Δ. In modern terms this is cardinal interpolation by entire functions. Problem 4 uses the 'interrupted' arithmetic node set x = nθ, (1−n)θ, (1+n)θ, (2−n)θ, (2+n)θ, …, with x = θω.

(i) End of Example 2 (§48). The data are alternately f, −f, f, … on these nodes, and the result is y = f sin2ωπ / sin2nπ. Check: at ω = n it gives f; at ω = 1−n it gives −f; at ω = 1+n it gives f. With θ = 2π and f = sin2nπ this becomes y = sin x, so the interpolant is again the sine curve.

(ii) §49 (Cor. 1). Take θ = π and f = tan nπ. The data points then lie on y = tan x, since tan(k±n)π = ±tan nπ. The interpolating curve is not the tangent but
y = tan nπ·sin2x / sin2nπ = sin2x / (2cos²nπ) = sin2x / (1+cos2nπ).
It coincides with tan x exactly at x = ±(i±n)π. The construction returns the entire, sine-type interpolant, not the meromorphic function that generated the data.

(iii) §50 (Cor. 2). Inserting the closed form of Δ in Example 1 (data f, f, −f, −f, f, f, …) gives y = f sinωπ / sinnπ. With θ = π and f = sin nπ this is exactly the sine line.

(iv) §51 (Scholion). For the interrupted progression (Problem 4) the normaliser Δ is always expressible by sines, because its Beta factors pair up through the reflection formula Γ(a)Γ(1−a) = π/sin πa. For a genuine arithmetic progression (Problem 3), Δ = ∫ z^{n−ω−1}(1−z)^{n−ω−1} dz = B(a,a) with a = n−ω. With a = ν/λ and z = v^λ this becomes λ∫ v^{ν−1}dv / (1−v^λ)^{(λ−ν)/λ}, i.e. λ(ν/ν) in Euler's notation. This is Γ(a)²/Γ(2a), a 'highly transcendent quadrature' not reducible to angles. As illustration, Problem 3 with n = 1/2 and alternating data ±f gives
Δy / (2fω(1+2ω)) = Σ 4/((2k+1)² − 4ω²) = (π/2ω) tan ωπ,
so y = πf(1+2ω) tan ωπ / Δ. This is evidently not sin ωπ, even though the data, f at θ/2 and −f at 3θ/2 etc., are values of sin x for θ = π. Euler therefore re-derives the case through Problem 1's Newton-type expansion.

(v) §52 (Problem 5, setup). The odd interpolant is expanded as y = Aω + Bω(ω²−n²) + Cω(ω²−n²)(ω²−(1−n)²) + …. This is a Newton divided-difference series on the symmetric nodes ±n, ±(1−n), ±(1+n), …. The next page obtains A, B, C, … and a two-parameter series for sinωπ / sinnπ.
errors: No mathematical errors found in the displayed formulas. All checks pass: the alternating-node evaluations of f sin2ωπ / sin2nπ and f sinωπ / sinnπ, the identity tan nπ / sin2nπ = 1/(2cos²nπ) = 1/(1+cos2nπ), the substitution z = v^λ in Δ, and the sum Σ 4/((2k+1)² − 4ω²) = π tan(ωπ)/(2ω).

The claim that the Problem 3 interpolant is 'manifestly' not sin ωπ is asserted, not shown; it is plausible since y involves Γ(1−2ω)/Γ(1/2−ω)² times tan ωπ. Note also that Problem 4 with n = 1/2 has coalescing nodes and so is not literally the same data problem as Problem 3; the comparison is heuristic.

ideas.what: Interpolating alternating ±f data on nodes k±n by an infinite-product (Lagrange-type) formula yields f sin2ωπ / sin2nπ or f sinωπ / sinnπ
ideas.modern_name: Cardinal / Lagrange interpolation by entire functions of exponential type (sine-type interpolation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Whittaker (1915), Kotelnikov–Shannon sampling; Lagrange infinite interpolation; Euler precursors
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opuscula Analytica I, 1783; Opera Omnia I.15)

ideas.what: Points taken on y = tan x are interpolated by sin2x/(1+cos2nπ), not by tan x; the interpolant agrees with tan x only at the nodes
ideas.modern_name: Non-uniqueness of interpolation on infinite node sets; minimal-type entire interpolant versus meromorphic data source (cf. Carlson's theorem)

ideas.what: Normaliser Δ reduces to sines for the interrupted progression but is a central Beta integral B(a,a) for a true progression
ideas.modern_name: Euler reflection formula versus non-elementary Γ(a)²/Γ(2a)
ideas.where_published: E555; Euler's Beta-integral papers (e.g. E321-type notation (p/q))
Introductio in analysin infinitorum (1748), ch. X

ideas.what: Odd Newton-type series in ω with symmetric nodes ±n, ±(1−n), … to represent sinωπ / sinnπ
ideas.modern_name: Newton interpolation series on non-uniform symmetric nodes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Newton; Euler for this specific series

missed.claim: Euler explicitly observes that the same type of node data can be interpolated by different curves depending on the interpolation scheme (Problem 3 versus Problem 4, and tan versus sin2x/(1+cos2nπ)). This is an early awareness of the uniqueness problem for interpolation on infinite node sets, later settled by growth conditions (Carlson). It is likely noted in Opera Omnia commentary, but rarely cited in histories of uniqueness theorems.
missed.quote: puncta data erunt in linea tangentium; neque tamen ipsa curua inuenta erit linea tangentium
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Historical precedent for exponential-type selection in cardinal interpolation; of modest historiographic interest only.

deep.surprise_reason: Correct, elegant illustrations of infinite interpolation and of when Beta normalisers reduce to sines. The interpolation-uniqueness remark is a nice precursor but is printed in a known Euler paper.
transcription_corrections: 'Δ = λ(ν/λ)' should read 'Δ = λ(ν/ν)' in Euler's symbol notation, consistent with the integral λ∫ v^{ν−1}dv / (1−v^λ)^{(λ−ν)/λ}.
